source: Zollman (2007) The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities, Philosophy of Science 74:574-587
finding: Zollman imports the Bala-Goyal two-armed bandit model into philosophy of science. Agents pick the action they think best, see their own and neighbours' results, and update by Bayes. Core claim: a less connected community can be MORE reliable, but is slower.
numbers: Setup: world fixed in state 2 (new method better); priors uniform on the interior; 10,000 runs per network; sizes 2 to 12; learning is finished when all play A1 or all believe state 2 with p>0.9999. Result (read from figures, no table): cycle > wheel > complete in reliability at every size tested; complete graph fastest, cycle slowest.
quote: in some contexts, a community of scientists is, as a whole, more reliable when its members are less aware of their colleagues' experimental results
limits: Exact reliability values appear only in figures; the paper says absolute values depend on payoffs and should not be taken too seriously. Later shown parameter-fragile (a09, a10).
agent_relevance: Root of G4/S3: shared early results can lock a whole group onto a wrong answer; isolated attempts keep someone testing the right option.

source: Zollman (2007) The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities, Philosophy of Science 74:574-587
finding: Worked toy example of the mechanism: four doctors with priors 0.33, 0.49, 0.51, 0.66. Two test the new treatment and both get mildly negative results. After pooling, everyone drops it, although it is truly better.
numbers: Likelihood of each negative result is 0.4 if new is better, 0.6 if worse. Posteriors after pooling: 0.1796, 0.2992, 0.3163, 0.4632 (all below 0.5, so nobody pursues the new method). Probability of this misleading outcome when the new method is better: 0.16. If D had not seen C's result, her belief would stay 0.5621 and she would test again.
limits: Toy example, not a general model of science. Needs evidence that depends on what agents choose to test (active search) and an old option that is uninformative about the new one.
agent_relevance: Exact analogue of an agent dropping a good approach after one unlucky sample shared with peers. Misleading evidence spreads; isolated attempts re-test.

source: Zollman (2007) The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities, Philosophy of Science 74:574-587
finding: Why density hurts: all non-isomorphic networks of size 3 to 6 were tested. Density is the best single predictor of success; only the clustering coefficient adds anything. Degree inequality (the hub, or 'royal family') does NOT predict failure.
numbers: 10,000 trials per graph, sizes 3-6; regression on size-6 graphs: lower density and lower clustering mean higher successful learning; in-network degree variance uncorrelated with success. Cycle beat wheel at all sizes, so removing the hub does not fix it.
limits: Small sizes only (exhaustive search needs n<=6). Bala and Goyal's theorem was about a hub; Zollman shows total connectivity, not centrality, is the culprit.
agent_relevance: Number of channels matters more than who is central. A star-style orchestrator is not the main risk; everyone seeing everything is.

source: Zollman (2007) The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities, Philosophy of Science 74:574-587
finding: The mechanism is 'inertia'. In sparse networks bad runs stay local, so diversity of action is kept long enough for good evidence to arrive.
numbers: After A2 players get below-expectation results, about 4 times more agents change strategy in a highly connected network than in a sparse one. Given exactly one A2 player left, a dense network is almost 3 times as likely to have zero A2 players next round (100 runs: complete 6-network vs the most reliable 6-network).
limits: Statistics come from 100-run comparisons, not 10,000. Mechanism is one explanation; later work shows it needs hard problems (a09).
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a minority of attempts uninformed by others (G4, S3). Diversity is transient: isolation delays convergence, it does not replace evidence.

source: Zollman (2007) The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities, Philosophy of Science 74:574-587
finding: Robust speed-reliability trade-off: the structures that make the group more reliable also make it slower.
numbers: Average time to success was lowest for the complete graph, highest for the cycle, with the wheel between (Fig. 3). Footnote 7: ordering of cycle, wheel and complete held across changes to number of strategies and payoff gap.
quote: there is a robust trade-off between the reliability of a community and the speed with which it reaches a correct conclusion
limits: Footnote 7 robustness claim was later contradicted for pB above about 0.525 (a09). Speed is counted in rounds, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Isolation costs time. Pay for it only on hard items where first answers are often wrong.

source: Zollman (2025) Beliefs and Social Networks, Oxford Handbook of Belief (philsci-archive 25858)
finding: Zollman's 2025 review states the field's main lesson: no simple relation between network structure and belief. Whether more links help depends on the learning problem. Diversity of search helps on hard problems, not on easy ones.
numbers: Review covers information cascades, pooling (DeGroot, repeated majority), contagion, bandits, landscape search, argumentation, network formation. Names sparse networks as one social way to keep diversity (Zollman 2007, 2010b; Grim et al 2013; Wu 2023a). Others: stubborn priors, ignoring subcommunities, confirmation bias (Gabriel and O'Connor 2024).
quote: even very simple questions, like 'are more connections good or bad for the uptake of reliable beliefs?', do not have unequivocal answers
limits: Secondary source, written by the originator of the effect. Check claims against primaries.
agent_relevance: Gives the boundary rule: isolate only when the problem is hard; otherwise connectivity is harmless or helpful.

source: Zollman (2025) Beliefs and Social Networks, Oxford Handbook of Belief (philsci-archive 25858)
finding: Information cascade theory: fully rational agents who see predecessors' announcements can all converge on the wrong answer. Sharing can help each agent and hurt the group.
numbers: Lab confirmations cited: Anderson and Holt 1997, Hung and Plott 2001, Kubler and Weizsacker 2004/2005, Ziegelmeyer et al 2010. Groups do not use the information supplied. Subjects overpay for private information (Kubler and Weizsacker 2004). Stronger signals do not always break a cascade (Ziegelmeyer 2010). Cascades need bounded signals (Smith and Sorensen 2000).
limits: Cited second-hand; no numbers in the review. Cascades are sequential and observe actions only, unlike the bandit models.
agent_relevance: Sequential visibility of earlier answers (anchoring) is the cascade route in an LLM pipeline. Keep first attempts blind.

source: Zollman (2025) Beliefs and Social Networks, Oxford Handbook of Belief (philsci-archive 25858)
finding: Human lab tests of the search models: limiting information can sometimes improve group results by keeping behaviour diverse. Pooling experiments are mixed.
numbers: Supporting search experiments listed: Mason, Jones and Goldstone 2008; Mason and Watts 2012; Derex and Boyd 2016; Charness, Cooper and Grossman 2020; Wisdom, Song and Goldstone 2004; Goldstone et al 2013. Pooling: Becker, Brackbill and Centola 2017 and Brandts et al 2015 confirm bias toward well-connected people's initial guesses; Jonsson, Hahn and Olsson 2015 found a small-world net beat the complete net, against the pooling model.
limits: Review says 'sometimes'. Barkoczi and Galesic say Mason and Watts found the opposite direction (efficient networks won), see a13. Those papers were not opened by me.
agent_relevance: Human evidence is mixed; sparse-is-better is not a law.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner, O'Connor (2017) In Epistemic Networks, Is Less Really More? Phil Sci 84:234-252
finding: Main refutation of generality. The Zollman effect appears only when the problem is hard: few agents, small data batches, tiny gap between the two options. Elsewhere sparse nets only slow learning.
numbers: Zollman used pB=0.501 vs pA=0.5, n=1000 trials per round, size 10. Authors varied pB 0.501-0.7, n 1-6000, size 4-100, at least 10,000 runs each. The cycle-minus-complete success gap is 0 for pB>=0.525; at pB=0.51 the gap is under 2 percentage points. The effect never reversed.
quote: less connectivity can improve inquiry only in a small parameter range in which learning is especially difficult
limits: Same Bala-Goyal Bayesian model family. No reversal found, so the effect may exist but be too small to detect. Python code published with the paper.
agent_relevance: Strongest boundary condition: isolation helps on hard, noisy items; on easy items it is wasted effort. Gate isolation by a difficulty signal (links to G1).

source: Rosenstock, Bruner, O'Connor (2017) In Epistemic Networks, Is Less Really More? Phil Sci 84:234-252
finding: The effect grows when each round gives fewer trials (law of small numbers) and shrinks as the community grows.
numbers: Size 10, pB=0.51: the cycle-vs-complete gap is larger at low n (n tested 10 to 10,000). Size 100, pB=0.501, n=1000: complete net converges to the better action 99.12% vs 100% for the cycle, but mean convergence round is 20 (complete) vs 1,977 (cycle).
limits: Single parameter point reported for size 100. Speed in rounds.
agent_relevance: At large group sizes connecting loses almost nothing; about 100 times more rounds for under 1 point of reliability is a bad trade.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner, O'Connor (2017) In Epistemic Networks, Is Less Really More? Phil Sci 84:234-252
finding: Kummerfeld and Zollman (2016) found a reverse Zollman effect with epsilon-greedy agents: when agents explore more on their own, the complete network beats the cycle. Rosenstock et al show this effect also washes out.
numbers: Eight agents, cycle vs complete; worse action pays 0, better action drawn from a normal (mean 1, SD 9 in the original). Low epsilon (0.05): cycle better. High epsilon (0.35): complete better. Re-run with mean 1 to 4 and SD 3 and 9: network effects shrink as the mean rises and as SD falls, for both epsilons.
limits: Less extensive sweep than for the Bala-Goyal models (authors say so). The original Kummerfeld and Zollman paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Individual exploration substitutes for network sparsity. An agent that already samples diversely (temperature, forced alternatives) gains little from isolation and gains from sharing.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner, O'Connor (2017) In Epistemic Networks, Is Less Really More? Phil Sci 84:234-252
finding: Authors' reading of what survives: sparse networks reliably cost speed and rarely give accuracy benefits outside a narrow zone. They doubt such models can guide real policy without more testing.
numbers: Zollman 2010 (beta priors with a,b in [0,4], 10,000 rounds) reported the same ordering, cycle > wheel > complete; Rosenstock et al reproduce the ordering only at hard parameters. Zollman 2010 says the ordering 'remains the same'; the authors reply that the effect 'does not arise for significant portions of the relevant parameter space'.
limits: Mapping from model to real science is open; the paper says so itself.
agent_relevance: Do not cite 'more communication hurts' as general. Cite it as 'hard problems with small samples'.

source: Barkoczi, Galesic (2016) Social learning strategies modify the effect of network structure on group performance, Nat Commun 7:13109
finding: Reconciles two contradicting results: Lazer and Friedman (2007), where inefficient networks win, and Mason and Watts (2012), where efficient networks win. Which wins depends on the social learning rule.
numbers: 100 agents, rugged NK landscape (N=15; simple case K=0), 200 steps, 10 networks. Best-member copying (sample s=3): inefficient (long path) networks beat efficient ones; correlation of diameter with payoff r=0.83. Conformity copying (s=3): efficient networks win; r=-0.77. Conformity with small samples gives the best long-run payoff in complex environments; best-member copying is best in simple ones.
quote: If both strategy and network promote high levels of the same activity (either exploration or exploitation), performance is likely to drop
limits: Simulation; the human strategies in Mason and Watts are only inferred. The Lazer and Friedman and Mason and Watts papers were not opened by me.
agent_relevance: General principle: pair a fast-sharing rule with a slow network, or the reverse. If the agent copies the best answer, isolate more; if it uses majority conformity, connectivity is less harmful.

source: Weatherall, O'Connor (2020) Conformity in Scientific Networks, Synthese (arXiv 1803.09905)
finding: Adds a conformity preference to the bandit network model. More conformity means fewer accurate consensuses, more polarisation and more wrong outcomes.
numbers: Random graphs, N=10, pB=0.55, n=5, edge probability q=0.5. At k=0 about 96% of runs converge to the true consensus. At k=0.1 consensus of either sort appears in only about 16% of runs; correct outcomes 55%, incorrect 44% in the compared setting. Multi-armed bandits at large k: converge to the best arm 34% of the time with 3 arms, 25% with 4, 19% with 5, against over 88% at k=0. Wheel converges to the better action 57% of the time vs 87% for a comparison graph.
limits: The figure and column text extracted partly garbled; the k=0.1 55%/44% pair and the 57%/87% wheel pair are read from prose and should be checked against the paper before use.
agent_relevance: Copying neighbours for coordination alone (a model matching a majority) erodes truth-seeking. Supports G4 and G5.

source: Weatherall, O'Connor (2020) Conformity in Scientific Networks, Synthese (arXiv 1803.09905)
finding: Historical motivation for the conformity model: Semmelweis's hand-washing finding was rejected by peers although it cut deaths in his clinic.
numbers: First clinic death rate about 10% vs 3-4% in the midwives' clinic. Paper also cites Asch: conformity chosen about 30% of the time. Also cites star networks inhibiting successful belief (Williams 2017).
limits: Historical narrative, not a test. Williams 2017 not opened.
agent_relevance: Context only.

source: Bala, Goyal (1998) Learning from Neighbours, Review of Economic Studies 65:595-621 (as described in Zollman 2007)
finding: Founding formal model. Two states, two actions, Bayesian agents see neighbours' payoffs on a graph. On an infinite line, correct convergence is guaranteed under mild priors. Adding a 'royal family' connected to everyone gives a positive chance of wrong convergence.
numbers: No simulation numbers. Result as relayed: probability of wrong consensus is zero on the infinite line and above zero with a royal family, because bad royal results mislead everyone and A1 players then learn nothing.
limits: Described via Zollman 2007 (opened); the original paper was not opened. Theorem needs an infinite population.
agent_relevance: Theoretical root: a shared source of unlucky evidence can sink everyone.

source: Mayo-Wilson, Zollman, Danks (2011) The Independence Thesis: When Individual and Social Epistemology Diverge, Phil Sci 78:653-677
finding: Proves that individual and group epistemic rationality can come apart: rational individuals can form unreliable groups and the reverse, under four criteria.
numbers: No numbers obtained. Only the search-result abstract was seen; full text blocked (HTTP 403) in this session.
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified until read.
agent_relevance: Theoretical licence for designing the group-level protocol (G4) separately from single steps.

source: Lazer, Friedman (2007) The Network Structure of Exploration and Exploitation, Admin Sci Quarterly 52:667-694 (as summarised in Barkoczi and Galesic 2016)
finding: Agent-based rugged-landscape search. A locally connected lattice beats a fully connected network in the long run: slow spread keeps diversity.
numbers: No numbers obtained. Per Barkoczi and Galesic: agents used best-member copying; inefficient networks won.
limits: Not opened. Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Landscape-search version of the same effect.

source: Mason, Watts (2012) Collaborative learning in networks, PNAS 109:764-769 (as summarised in Barkoczi and Galesic 2016)
finding: Human experiment on eight network structures: efficient networks outperformed inefficient ones, opposing Lazer and Friedman. Participants copied more when 2 or 3 of 3 neighbours had a solution.
numbers: No N obtained. Per Barkoczi and Galesic: efficient networks superior; individuals in efficient networks explored more, not less.
limits: Not opened. Details unverified.
agent_relevance: A human counterexample: with conformist copying, connectivity helped.

source: Shen, Liu, Dai et al (2025) Understanding the Information Propagation Effects of Communication Topologies in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems, EMNLP 2025 main 623
finding: Clean LLM test of the Zollman trade-off by counterfactual injection. Dense graphs spread a planted error more; sparse graphs pass a planted correct insight less. Best accuracy at moderate sparsity.
numbers: MMLU, six GPT-3.5 agents with distinct roles. 500 originally-correct questions: one agent forced wrong; going from Full to Chain cuts the effect by up to 19%. 500 originally-incorrect questions: one agent given the right answer; going from Chain to Full raises the effect by 10.5%. Their learned topology (EIB-Learner) averages 91.38% over six benchmarks vs at most 85.53% for the best predefined topology (LLM-Debate); MMLU 88.90 vs vanilla 80.39.
limits: One model (GPT-3.5), one benchmark for the propagation analysis, agents are role-prompted so not independent. Percentages are relative changes in the paper's TCTE measure.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence for a middle path: sparse links around unreliable agents, dense links around reliable ones.

source: Han, Tan, Yu et al (2026) Conformity Dynamics in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: The Roles of Topology and Self-Social Weighting (arXiv 2601.05606)
finding: LLM agents on a misinformation task: denser networks converge faster and here were slightly MORE accurate on average, but raise the risk of wrong-but-sure cascades when early signals are biased.
numbers: Seven agents, 448 claims (252 false, 196 true); ring (m=2) to complete (m=6). GPT-3.5 with peer weight 0.25: final accuracy 0.70 (ring) to 0.75 (complete). Sparse rings start at conformity index 0.55-0.65 and need six or more rounds to reach unanimity; denser (m>=4) converge faster. Star: central accuracy follows hub competence, with same-model alignment bias.
quote: increased network connectivity speeds up convergence but also heightens the risk of wrong-but-sure cascades
limits: Preprint. Binary task, authors' confidence-normalised pooling rule rather than free debate. Result contradicts a Zollman-style accuracy gain for sparsity.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to a blanket isolation rule: on a binary judgement with confidence weighting, connection added about 5 points.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2509.05396)
finding: Debate among LLMs can lower accuracy over rounds even when stronger models are the majority. Agents flip from correct to wrong to agree with peers.
numbers: MMLU, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K; mixed groups of GPT-4o-mini, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B; 100 random samples, 5 seeds. Accuracy often falls as rounds progress, most on MMLU and CSQA. Correct-to-wrong flip rate is highest when the agent is alone in its answer and falls as more peers agree. A correctness-payoff prompt did not reduce harmful flips.
quote: favoring agreement over challenging flawed reasoning
limits: Small samples (100). Debate is all-see-all, the dense end of the Zollman axis. Sycophancy and conformity are named as causes, not isolated by a network manipulation.
agent_relevance: The dense end hurts in practice. A lone correct answer gets overwritten by peer text (G4, G5).

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs? NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv 2508.17536)
finding: Majority voting over independent first answers gets most of the gain attributed to multi-agent debate. Debate is a martingale in their model: it does not raise expected correctness.
numbers: Seven benchmarks, Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B, five agents, 2, 3 and 5 rounds; also Qwen2.5-32B. Decentralised, Sparse and Centralised debate compared against majority voting (T=0). Majority voting is on par with debate in most cases. Theorem 2: expected belief in the correct answer is unchanged by a debate round. Biasing updates toward correction helps.
quote: debate alone does not improve expected correctness
limits: Table 1 numbers not extracted by me. Model assumes Bayesian-style symmetric updating; homogeneous agents only.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM support for independent attempts plus code-side voting: the interaction step adds little, so isolation loses little (S3, G5).

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate (arXiv 2305.14325)
finding: Original claim that debate helps: three ChatGPT agents, two rounds, beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on math and chess.
limits: Weak models. Choi et al 2025 and Wynn et al 2025 later find most of the gain is voting, or loss with mixed groups. On GSM8K voting was within 4 points of debate with overlapping standard errors.
agent_relevance: Baseline for judging any interaction step: the debate gain over plain voting was large on arithmetic and small on GSM8K.

source: Zollman (2025) Beliefs and Social Networks, Oxford Handbook of Belief (philsci-archive 25858)
finding: Exploration is a public good: each agent pays the cost of trying a possibly worse option while the group gains, so individuals under-explore. Group-level design (sparse links) is one remedy, but it slows consensus and can promote polarisation.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Bolton and Harris 1999, Kummerfeld and Zollman 2016 for under-exploration; Wu and O'Connor 2023 for polarisation cost of diversity-preserving structure.
limits: Review; cited papers not opened.
agent_relevance: The scaffold should force the diversity the model will not produce alone (distinct fresh attempts), rather than rely on the model to explore. Forced diversity is code-side, consistent with section 1 of the schema.
